description: This cluster encompasses research examining the psychological and emotional dimensions of human interaction with artificial intelligence, emphasising how these dynamics shape trust, attitudes, and personality-related responses. A core lies in understanding how individuals perceive and engage with AI-driven technologies, and how the mentioned psychological mechanisms, such as trust, emotional attachment, and perceived control, determine acceptance or resistance. Youn and Jin (2021) investigated the usage of parasocial relationships and symbolic companionship with AI, processes that can strengthen trust and foster a sense of emotional connection. They highlight the role of perceived trustworthiness in shaping human AI bonds. Extending this line of inquiry, Matthews et  al. (2021) examine personality-driven responses to AI, showing that traits such as neuroticism predict resistance, while openness and extraversion foster acceptance. Other studies have concentrated on AI’s integration in work and consumer contexts. Gessl et  al. (2019) and Huo et  al. (2022) explored how human AI collaboration influences group identity, symbolic consumption, and perceived control factors that can exacerbate discomfort or anxiety, especially among individuals high in neuroticism. In applied domains, research on AI in healthcare and eldercare further demonstrates how trust in medical AI systems is established, a concern particularly salient for individuals predisposed to health-related anxiety or scepticism towards technology (Park & Woo, 2022; Savela et  al., 2022). Collectively, this body of work underscores that neurotic individuals may experience heightened concerns regarding AI integration due to their emotional sensitivity and risk perceptions. This cluster thus provides a critical foundation for investigating how personality traits such as neuroticism that moderates human responses to artificial intelligence.

This cluster draws attention to how humans perceive, interact with, and attribute personality-like qualities to AI and robotic systems, focusing on mechanisms such as anthropomorphism, social cognition, and emotional evaluation. A recurring theme is the projection of human traits onto AI, which shapes whether people find such technologies approachable, trustworthy, or unsettling. Nicolas and Agnieszka (2021) explained how cognitive tendencies and personality differences influence anthropomorphic perceptions, shedding light on why some individuals develop an affinity towards robots while others feel discomfort patterns that resonate strongly with neurotic predispositions. Similarly, Chang et  al. (2018) elaborate how features such as humour, vocal tone, and expressiveness affect perceptions of robots likability, especially in socially sensitive contexts like eldercare and personal assistance. Issues of control and uniqueness also figure prominently. Stein et  al. (2019) illustrated that apprehensions about diminished autonomy or being replaced by machines underlie resistance to AI, anxieties particularly pronounced among individuals high in neuroticism. Additional work extends these insights: Mirnig et  al. (2016), Paetzel-Prüsmann et  al. (2021) and von Davier (2018) investigate children’s interactions with AI and the integration of AI into educational assessment and creative processes, pointing to the early development of attitudes and the broader societal reach of automated systems. Overall, this cluster emphasises that likability, anthropomorphic cues, and control dynamics are pivotal in shaping psychological responses to AI. It suggests that individuals characterised by higher levels of neuroticism may be especially susceptible to aversion, unease, and anxiety in their encounters with robots and intelligent systems.

This cluster focuses on the interconnection between personality traits, cognitive functioning, and social behaviour, drawing on psychological assessments, predictive modelling, and situational analyses. The research demonstrates how differences in mental processes, curiosity, belief systems, and interpersonal dynamics shape how personality is expressed and enacted in everyday life. Alessandri et  al. (2015) highlight the neurological roots of personality, showing that EEGalpha asymmetry is linked to traits associated with positivity, thereby connecting brain activity with dispositional tendencies. Chapman et  al. (2016) add a methodological dimension, employing statistical learning and high-dimensional models to refine the measurement and prediction of personality, with implications for anticipating outcomes across diverse life domains. Interpersonal mechanisms also emerge as critical. Clifton and Webster (2017) and Kashdan et  al. (2018) analyse how gossip, situational cues, and social processes actively shape personality expression, revealing how external environments and social exchanges reinforce or challenge traits. From a longitudinal and network perspective, Nestler et  al. (2015), Parrigon et  al. (2017) and Peng et  al. (2015) provide multi-level analytic approaches that trace personality development across individuals, dyads, and social groups. Taken together, this body of work demonstrates that personality is dynamic and contextually embedded, influenced not only by stable cognitive dispositions but also by the evolving social environments in which individuals operate.

This cluster highlights how individual differences in personality, attitudes, and anxiety shape the development of trust in artificial intelligence and robotic systems, particularly in domains such as education and the workplace. The literature points to the psychological conditions that drive acceptance, hesitation, and compliance in AI-mediated interactions, offering insight into the ways emotions and cognition guide responses to these technologies. Kanero et  al. (2022) show that cultural and personality variations significantly influence whether people approach Similarly, studies by Latikka et  al. (2021) and Maggi et  al. (2021) reveal that autonomy and perceived control are decisive factors in shaping trust: users express more confidence when they feel in charge, while those high in neuroticism often react negatively to the uncertainty and loss of control associated with autonomous systems. Oksanen et  al. (2020) and Reich-Stiebert and Eyssel (2015) investigate the use of AI-based tutoring systems, showing how personality traits, anxieties, and attitudes influence students’ trust and willingness to learn with robotic instructors. Adding to this, Sindermann et  al. (2022) examine how AI communication styles alter user performance, compliance, and distraction, further demonstrating that personality traits – including neuroticism – mediate engagement with AI in structured tasks. Collectively, the scholarship suggests that trust in AI is contingent upon personality-linked psychological processes, particularly sensitivity to uncertainty and fear of reduced control. For neurotic individuals, these tendencies translate into more pronounced scepticism and anxiety in AI-driven environments.

This cluster investigates the application of artificial intelligence, cyberpsychology, and social network analysis in advancing the understanding of personality disorders and associated psychological traits, with a particular emphasis on neuroticism and interpersonal dysfunction. Research within this theme underscores the utilisation of AI-driven methodologies and network-based frameworks to improve the assessment and conceptualisation of complex personality disorders such as borderline personality disorder (BPD) and psychopathy. Ancis (2020) offers a critical examination of cyberpsychology, elucidating how AI and digital technologies are fundamentally transforming the study of human behaviour and personality within virtual environments. Beeney et  al. (2018) analyse BPD through social network dynamics, demonstrating how social disadvantages and unstable relationships exacerbate personality pathology, thereby illuminating the intricate links between neuroticism and interpersonal challenges. Eichstaedt et  al. (2021) and Fan and Chang (2010) rigorously evaluate the psychometric validity of AI-derived personality assessments, raising important questions regarding the fidelity of AI systems in accurately capturing traits like neuroticism through chatbot-mediated interactions and text analytics. Complementing these insights, Lazarus et  al. (2020) provide an authoritative review of linguistic analysis techniques, specifically closed- and open-vocabulary methods, offering methodological guidance to enhance the reliability of AI-based personality research. McCuish et  al. (2019) apply social network analysis to elucidate the symptomatology of borderline and psychopathic personality traits, illustrating how computational approaches can reveal underlying structural patterns within personality disorders. Collectively, this cluster emphasises the transformative potential of integrating AI and social network methodologies to unravel the complexities of personality disorders, while also acknowledging critical ethical and practical considerations in AI-driven psychological evaluation.

This cluster investigates the intersection of artificial intelligence, computational linguistics, and psychological measurement, emphasising the deployment of machine learning and sophisticated text analytic methods to evaluate mental health status, personality traits, and moral cognition. It also critically examines the methodological complexities inherent in such approaches, including issues of algorithmic bias, construct validity, and ethical accountability. He et  al. (2017) exemplify the application of natural language processing (NLP) and text mining in the automated detection of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), demonstrating AI’s capacity to extract meaningful psychological indicators from self-narrative data. Kennedy and Guzmán (2021) explore the extent to which moral values and personality constructs are encoded in linguistic behaviour, highlighting language as a rich, implicit medium for psychological inference. Kern et  al. (2016) Offer an incisive critique of the methodological challenges and potential pitfalls associated with leveraging social media text for large-scale personality and mental health assessments, underscoring both the promise and the constraints of AI-driven text mining in psychological science. Schouw et  al. (2020) employ network analytic techniques to map the enduring influence of childhood experiences on adult personality development, advancing understanding of the longitudinal impact of early environmental factors on traits such as neuroticism. Focused (Tay et  al., 2020, 2022) foreground the critical issues surrounding machine-learning measurement bias (MLMB) in AI-based personality diagnostics, advocating for rigorous frameworks to detect, mitigate, and prevent bias while safeguarding psychometric robustness and ethical standards in AI-enabled psychological tools. Collectively, these works underscore the transformative potential of AI-facilitated language processing in psychological assessment, while emphasising the imperative for methodological rigour and ethical vigilance in harnessing these emerging technologies.

This cluster critically examines the integral role of social network structures in shaping personality traits, behavioural evolution, and interpersonal processes. It foregrounds the influence of social positioning, peer group dynamics, and ecological factors in moulding fundamental personality attributes such as self-regulation, adaptability, and social engagement. Clifton and Webster (2017) position social network analysis (SNA) as a vital analytical tool for decoding how an individual’s relational embeddedness within social systems influences personality formation and behavioural outcomes. Duckworth et  al. (2018) provide nuanced insights into the emergence of adaptive behaviours, highlighting how individuals strategically navigate structural constraints and opportunities that arise from the interplay between personality maturation and social interactions. Franken et  al. (2016) emphasise the formative impact of peer relationships in early adolescence, illustrating how social affiliations contribute to the manifestation and modulation of externalising behaviours, thereby underscoring the salience of social context in personality expression and behavioural control. From an ethological perspective, Hasenjager and Dugatkin (2015) elucidate how social structures govern interactional patterns, advancing an evolutionary framework for understanding the adaptation and persistence of social behaviours across diverse environments. Kornienko et  al. (2020) explore the causal pathways linking social rejection to antisocial conduct, rigorously testing the confluence model to reveal how experiences of exclusion catalyse shifts in behavioural repertoires. Selden and Goodie (2018) synthesise evidence on the bidirectional relationship between Five-Factor Model (FFM) personality dimensions and social network architecture, demonstrating how personality traits both shape and are shaped by individuals’ social perceptions and network positions. Collectively, these studies illuminate the dynamic and reciprocal processes through which social network configurations and personality development co-evolve, providing a comprehensive understanding of the social underpinnings of personality.

This cluster critically explores the convergence of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and digital communication in the context of personality assessment and user experience design. It examines how AI-powered tools are increasingly leveraged to infer personality traits, facilitate human–AI interaction, and shape psychological outcomes in digital environments. Chen and Lin (2017) illustrate the efficacy of automated personality inference through linguistic behaviour, demonstrating how machine learning algorithms can predict traits such as neuroticism based on individuals’ written language. Fatahi and Moradi (2016) introduce a fuzzy cognitive map framework designed to evaluate user desirability through personality profiling, highlighting the role of AI in delivering adaptive, user-centred experiences in digital education systems. Mou and Xu (2017) interrogate the phenomenon of media inequality by contrasting user engagement in human–human versus human–AI interactions, offering valuable insights into how individuals socially interpret and respond to AI-mediated communication. Savci et  al. (2022) apply predictive modelling to examine problematic social media use (PSU), establishing a connection between excessive online behaviour and personality dimensions like neuroticism, and emphasising the psychological costs associated with digital overexposure. Collectively, this thematic cluster sheds light on the evolving role of AI in both assessing personality and mediating digital interaction, while drawing attention to the psychological, behavioural, and ethical implications of increasingly personalised, AI-driven online ecosystems.
